Homeless a growing problem

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
The numbers of people living on the streets has increased globally during the Covid pandemic and the City of Cape Town that survives on its glossy tourism image is looking very shabby. There are 14 300 homeless people in Cape Town and only 2000 beds in homeless shelters. Tent towns have sprung up everywhere – there are tents clinging to the Greenpoint tennis courts fence, homeless people are living under bridges, between the highway and in the parks. There are no doubt more homeless but is it because they are just not having to remove their structures everyday?

Summary:
Rate paying residents are getting fed up of stepping over human faeces on the pavements, avoiding needles to say not nothing of the increasing public indecency. But not every person living on the streets is a drug addict and a criminal and NGO’s that run shelters are asking is the R744 million spent on this societal challenge could be better spent? R286 million of which is spent on criminal justice costs alone.
7 Street people represented Ndifuna Ukwazi Law Centre launched applications in both the Western Cape High Court and the Equality Court challenging the constitutionality and discriminatory impact of two of the City’s municipal by-laws relating to streets, public places and the prevention of noise nuisances (2007) and the Integrated Waste Management By-law (2009) criminalise homelessness. What these laws highlight is the incredible violence towards the homeless. Their shelters and possessions are considered waste and get confiscated regularly, they also can’t eat, beg, urinate in public yet there are no toilets provided. Uturn report reveals that more money is spent on criminalising the homeless than providing long term solutions, and they not winning the war.


Further information:
The City of Cape Town despite these laws is actually more proactive that other cities, and have a budget allocated and have various Safe Spaces and dedicated departments. But more money is spent removing baboons and keeping them out of residential areas than on the homeless, if one compares the per baboon with person spend . The upgrade to the Seapoint promenade was R16.9 million and the City’s homesless budget is R30 million
The COVID Strandfontein experience has changed the City viewpoint to some degree and the homeless have formed an action group and together with service providers are engaging with the City. The homeless for the first time have an active voice in the City. It’s a complex problem - the insert will speak to the NGO’s grappling with the issues, the homeless, the rate paying residents and the City officials

Script:


Script: Cape Town’s homelessness is a controversial issue, with shelters springing up between highways and in public spaces. When UCT, and Table Mountain were set ablaze from an unattended cooking fire, it released toxic vitriol on social media, from the public towards the homeless.
Link “ Cities around the world are dealing with the extremely complex issue of people who find themselves homeless, and the impact of Covid has put many more on the streets. Cape Town is no different, with 14 and half thousand people living rough and shelter for just 2 and half thousand
Script: These startling statistics were revealed in a UTurn Homeless Ministries report on the cost of homelessness in Cape Town, co authored by COO Jon Hopkins, and 2 other organizations. He says we are reacting to the problem, rather than solving it.
Jon: In South Africa all cities are doing something a bit different and Cape Town has budget towards homelessness other cities, Tshwane have a lovely policy, but no budget, Johannesburg doesn't have a budget. Durban has no budget.
Script. And most of the support for the homeless is coming out of the pockets of Capetonians, but is it changing the situation? 50% of the people who are homeless, have been so for over 8 years, and they have mental physical and substance abuse problems, and the common narrative, is that people are choosing to live on the streets
UPSOUND
Jon three percent of those that we asked said, no, I choose to be on the streets some other people said, no, it's a choice, but also I faced abuse at home, or my house had 37 people living in it and there was no space and I was living in the backyard ..I'm choosing to be here because at least then I feel like I'm in control of the situation.
Script: Anda Mazantsana is a classic example, he started living on the streets when he left a children's home, surviving as a parking attendant on Tafelberg road, for the last 8 years. It’s people’s disdain, that hurts him the most
Anda “You are seen as a sort of animal because you are seen different from the next person you are looked at as trash. You are like a nobody. You don't exist
Script: In was major depression that drove Carin Gelderbloem out onto the streets
Carin: I had a comfortable life. I am a qualified hairstylist what happened was my husband passed away suddenly. I was also very depressed and I just isolated myself from the world
Script: She stayed in a shelter for a couple of months until she was forced to move on. Carin lived here in drain pipe in the Company Gardens
Carin “The 9 almost 10 years that I was on the street. I never sat once on a bench and begged I would go at night, when the traders are busy packing up their stuff on Greenmarket square and I would pick up the beads that they would drop and I would make bracelets or whatever
Script: Since lockdown, settlements have sprung up everywhere, as people are no longer hiding themselves, and removing their structures before the City confiscates them. But ratepayers are irate, complaining about anti-social behaviour, and that their property is devaluing. Part of the problem is that a high percentage of homeless people, have major mental illnesses and aren't getting help.
Link “One of the biggest problems for the homeless, and the public is that access to toilets is limited and so human waste on the streets becomes a problem. Here in Observatory they provided these ablution facilities that has reduced the problem by 75%
Script: In Observatory there are 80 homeless residents, and the OBSID treads a fine line between angry business owners, and those who believe the homeless have a right to be there. Amanda Kirk says there is no silver bullet, but they have work programs, health support, and a sponsored house
Amanda “Somebody's always angry with us So what we try to do is we try to say people are going to be living on the streets. We're going to try and minimize the impact on the public space. And the toilets is a perfect example of that. The second thing we do ..Once the business is closed at night, They'll go and sleep in doorways. Our public safety team goes out every morning and we will ask people to move the our workbased rehab team comes out and do a daily clean up of refuse that is generated by people living on the streets.
Link: What strikes you the most when you engage with people who find themselves homeless is the level of violence that they have to endure
Script: Carlos Mesquita became homeless 6 years ago when his drug problem destroyed his music career. He had won several SAMA awards, and travelled the world, before he learnt to scavenge from bins for goods to sell
Carlos “ I became the first homeless person to ever get a stand on the parade. But they came and they started throwing all my stuff onto the truck. They just took the tent with everything that was in it and they threw me onto the floor. And one CCID and one law enforcement did this to my eyes and each of them like a canister of pepper spray in my eyes. Believe me you can't lay a charge, believe me, you can but nobody is going to follow it up and nobody's even going to take that charge.
Carin: Even if you go to SAPs with a complaint they would ask you- but why you sleeping outside . When Ramees my partner was stabbed it was drunk kids school children. They were throwing boulders on our tent they were kicking people off the benches they were hitting people with buckles in their faces
Script: Driven out of the Company Gardens she paid the security to sleep at the reservoir in Oranjezicht
Carin “Law enforcement came and they took my stuff. Claire: What things your possessions
Carin My jewellery that I make, my ID, my bank cards, my bottom dentures
Script: Carin became the face of the homeless when along with 7 others, she took on the Cities bylaws after she was fined R500 for littering and dumping at 3am, when she was sleeping in this park.
Carin They want to fine us, where are we going to get the money do they want us to become criminals to get the money to stay out of jail
Script: They won an interim protection order in 2019 but now Ndifuna Ukwazi Law Centre has escalated it to the Western Cape High Court, and the Equality Court. They are challenging the constitutionality, and discriminatory impact of two of the bylaws, says Jonnty Cogger.
Jonty: It's never justified to criminalize homelessness. Homeless people are really a vulnerable sector or members of community, criminalization perpetuates the systemic disadvantage. It violates their right to property, freedom of movement
Script: The City has responded by sending out a questionnaire requesting residents to lodge their complaints against the homeless, and are looking at extending the powers of law enforcement, to arrest and remove people. Councillor Zahir Badrodien of Community Services and Health, jointly sent out the questionnaire with law Enforcement
Badroodien “It gets to a point where it's very clear that a homeless person will continue to refuse assistance from the City of Cape Town. And the city then also has a responsibility to enforce its bylaws that are able to keep our streets, our parks, our public spaces clean and free of obstruction for the benefit of all Capetonins
Jon “ Let's stop passing the problem around, where were you clearing them to? Someone else's neighborhood, to make it someone else's problem.
Claire: Is the fine the way to go?
Badrodien “fines are always the very last resort. But an additional program that the City of Cape Town is investing in is what we are calling the restoration program. We were able to work with a homeless person that has been identified at risk of potentially being fined to get them into a program and hopefully services before they even get to the court.
Link: 45% of the 744 million rand that is spent on the homeless is spent chasing them away, arresting them and putting them in prison, and only 16% of that money is spent on long term solutions.
Script: Like Carlos who spent 6 months awaiting trial in prison for having a trolley, despite being in possession of a letter from the chain store.
Jon: The current response is not working. It's broken. We need to push for one that does using programs that do work and use that rehabilitative long term process that actually ultimately is more cost effective.
Script: Rehabilitating people takes at least 18 months, but then there is an 80% chance they won't return to the streets. Currently a person is on the street for 8 and half years costing on average R455 000 compared to the R120 000, for a rehab program, and a critical part of this is appropriate accommodation
Anda “Once you have a roof over your head, you are able to think straight and.companies that are hiring, they look at you differently rather than from a person that will wash from the mountain and then try to go and get jobs
Script: Anda, Carlos, and Carin’s lives have changed dramatically in the last 9 months when they were provided with sponsored accommodation along with 28 others. Anda has got a part time job and is rewriting his matric. 87 % of the residents have found work and Carin runs a jewellery stall.
But the funding for the accommodation has run out, so Carlos has founded an NPO called the rehousing collective, providing an alternative housing model, and is fighting desperately to stop 31 people, returning to the street or the shelters
Carlos “ I'm the very first person to say to you that people will refuse to go into shelters and then people get very upset. But why? How could they refuse it? Because if you haven't been in a shelter, don't ask me that question
Script: Shelters only provide a bed for 3 months, after that they lose their funding from the Province. They don’t accept families, couples are separated, and anyone who is still struggling with substance issues - won’t get shelter. The City has two safe spaces but their policies are the same, and have only recently been upgraded to include showers.
Anda “Now to go back to square one again, it will be a disaster, because that's a promise that I made to myself once I went out of the streets that I would never want to see that life again.
